studies.title: High-Fat-Diet-Induced Kidney Injury in Rats: The Role of Tart Cherry Supplementation.
studies.abstract: The kidney plays a crucial role in the complex inter-organ communication that occurs during obesity, leading to the development of oxidative stress, inflammation, and fibrosis. Dysfunction of the transient receptor potential (TRP) ion channels contributes to this pathophysiology. This study was designed to evaluate the effects of antioxidant-rich fruit tart cherry (Prunus cerasus L.) on kidney morphology and protein expression in rats with diet-induced obesity (DIO). Methods include histological staining and immunohistochemical and Western blot assays. Obese rodents were fed with seed powder (DS) and seed powder plus juice (DJS) of the tart cherry. Results demonstrated that rats fed a high-fat-diet (HFD) showed a significant reduction in renal expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokines interleukin-1 beta (IL-1β) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) following tart cherry supplementation. Furthermore, the study provided evidence that TRP channels, specifically TRP canonical 1 (TRPC1) and TRP melastatin 2 (TRPM2), were significantly upregulated in obese animals (p < 0.05 vs. CHOW rats) and markedly downregulated following tart cherry supplementation (p < 0.05 vs. DIO rats). In conclusion, these TRP proteins offer new insights for identifying targets and biomarkers for developing therapeutic strategies against HFD-induced renal damage, characterized by glomerulosclerosis, fibrosis, and inflammation. Tart cherries supplementation exerted a protective effect on the kidneys by reducing protein oxidation and pro-inflammatory cytokine expression.

studies.title: Dysfunction of the Brown Adipose Organ in HFD-Obese Rats and Effect of Tart Cherry Supplementation.
studies.abstract: Obesity has a great impact on adipose tissue biology, based on its function as a master regulator of energy balance. Brown adipose tissue (BAT) undergoes remodeling, and its activity declines in obese subjects due to a whitening process. The anti-obesity properties of fruit extracts have been reported. The effects of tart cherry against oxidative stress, inflammation, and the whitening process in the BAT of obese rats were investigated. Intrascapular BAT (iBAT) alterations and effects of Prunus cerasus L. were debated in rats fed for 17 weeks with a high-fat diet (DIO), in DIO supplemented with seed powder (DS), and with seed powder plus the juice (DJS) of tart cherry compared to CHOW rats fed with a normo-caloric diet. iBAT histologic observations revealed a whitening process in DIO rats that was reduced in the DS and DJS groups. A modulation of uncoupling protein-1 (UCP-1) protein and gene expression specifically were detected in the obese phenotype. An upregulation of UCP-1 and related thermogenic genes after tart cherry intake was detected compared to the DIO group. Metabolic adjustment, endoplasmic reticulum stress, protein carbonylation, and the inflammatory microenvironment in the iBAT were reported in DIO rats. The analysis demonstrated an iBAT modulation that tart cherry promoted. In addition to our previous results, these data confirm the protective impact of tart cherry consumption on obesity.

studies.title: Anti-Inflammatory and Antioxidant Properties of Tart Cherry Consumption in the Heart of Obese Rats.
studies.abstract: Obesity is a risk factor for cardiovascular diseases, frequently related to oxidative stress and inflammation. Dietary antioxidant compounds improve heart health. Here, we estimate the oxidative grade and inflammation in the heart of dietary-induced obese (DIO) rats after exposure to a high-fat diet compared to a standard diet. The effects of tart cherry seed powder and seed powder plus tart cherries juice were explored. Morphological analysis and protein expressions were performed in the heart. The oxidative status was assessed by the measurement of protein oxidation and 4-hydroxynonenal in samples. Immunochemical and Western blot assays were performed to elucidate the involved inflammatory markers as proinflammatory cytokines and cellular adhesion molecules. In the obese rats, cardiomyocyte hypertrophy was accompanied by an increase in oxidative state proteins and lipid peroxidation. However, the intake of tart cherries significantly changed these parameters. An anti-inflammatory effect was raised from tart cherry consumption, as shown by the downregulation of analyzed endothelial cell adhesion molecules and cytokines compared to controls. Tart cherry intake should be recommended as a dietary supplement to prevent or counteract heart injury in obese conditions.

studies.title: Tart Cherry Juice and Seeds Affect Pro-Inflammatory Markers in Visceral Adipose Tissue of High-Fat Diet Obese Rats.
studies.abstract: Tart cherries ( This study has investigated the potential positive effects of tart cherries on rats with Diet-Induced Obesity (DIO). In particular, the inflammatory status in retroperitoneal (RPW) and perigonadal (PGW) adipose tissue were studied. Rats were fed  No differences in the weight of RPW and PGW animals were found between DS and DJS groups compared to DIO rats. However, an increase of inflammatory markers was observed in DIO group in comparison with control lean rats. A modulation of these markers was evident upon tart cherry supplementation. Study results suggest that tart cherry enriched-diet did not modify the accumulation of visceral fat, but it decreased inflammatory markers in both tissues. Therefore, this supplementation could be useful, in combination with healthy lifestyles, to modify adipose tissue cell metabolism limiting-obesity related organ damage.

studies.title: Effects of Tart Cherry Powder on Serum Uric Acid in Hyperuricemia Rat Model.
studies.abstract: Hyperuricemia, as a critical risk factor for various adverse clinical outcomes, shows a trend of increasing prevalence among young-aged population. Dietary adjuvant therapy by function foods, such as tart cherry, is promising. Thus, effects of tart cherry powder specialized in hyperuricemia were explored via establishing a hyperuricemia model in Sprague Dawley rats by cotreatment with oteracil potassium and adenine. The results indicated that low dose of tart cherry powder (0.17 g/kg·bw) showed effects on hyperuricemia by slightly decreasing serum uric acid and improving kidney injury, whereas high dose of tart cherry powder (0.50 g/kg·bw) could merely alleviate kidney injury. Meanwhile, adenosine deaminase activity rather than xanthine oxidase activity was affected at low dose, which reveals low dose of tarty cherry powder may be beneficial to hyperuricemia through reduction of ADA activity, and its reported potentials on antioxidation or anti-inflammation provide clues for further study.

studies.title: Effect of Tart Cherry Polyphenols on Osteoclast Differentiation and Activity.
studies.abstract: Bone is maintained by an intricate balance between bone formation and bone resorption. The presence of inflammation can contribute to an imbalance in bone homeostasis by enhancing differentiation and activity of osteoclasts, the cells that participate in the breakdown of bone. Polyphenols such as flavonoids found in plant-derived foods have been shown to have anti-inflammatory effects in various tissues. Tart cherries are a rich source of such polyphenolic compounds. Using mouse macrophage cells (RAW 264.7), we examined whether tart cherry polyphenols could dose dependently inhibit the proliferation and activity of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL) differentiated osteoclasts under inflammatory conditions. Tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) activity and staining of TRAP-positive multinucleated cells, used as indicators of osteoclast differentiation and activity, tended to decrease with tart cherry polyphenols treatment. Osteoprotegerin expression by osteoclasts was decreased in a similar manner. A significant increase in nitrite concentration was observed with the lower doses of tart cherry polyphenols of 50 and 100 μg/mL (P < .05). However, higher doses of tart cherry polyphenols (200 and 300 μg/mL) reduced nitrite concentrations below that of the control that received no tart cherry polyphenols treatment (P < .05). Western blot analyses showed that protein expression of cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) followed a similar trend, although results were not statistically significant. On the other hand, tart cherry polyphenols treatments dose dependently increased inducible nitric oxide synthase protein expression, with statistical significance noted at doses of 200 and 300 μg/mL. Overall, our findings suggest that the polyphenols associated with tart cherries potentially inhibit osteoclast differentiation and activity, which may be beneficial to bone health.

studies.title: Brain alterations in high fat diet induced obesity: effects of tart cherry seeds and juice.
studies.abstract: Evidence suggests that obesity adversely affects brain function. High body mass index, hypertension, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, and diabetes are risk factors for increasing cognitive decline. Tart cherries (PrunusCerasus L.) are rich in anthocyanins and components that modify lipid metabolism. This study evaluated the effects of tart cherries on the brain in diet-induced obese (DIO) rats. DIO rats were fed with a high-fat diet alone or in association with a tart cherry seeds powder (DS) and juice (DJS). DIO rats were compared to rats fed with a standard diet (CHOW). Food intake, body weight, fasting glycemia, insulin, cholesterol, and triglycerides were measured. Immunochemical and immunohistochemical techniques were performed. Results showed that body weight did not differ among the groups. Blood pressure and glycemia were decreased in both DS and DJS groups when compared to DIO rats. Immunochemical and immunohistochemical techniques demonstrated that in supplemented DIO rats, the glial fibrillary acid protein expression and microglial activation were reduced in both the hippocampus and in the frontal cortex, while the neurofilament was increased. Tart cherry intake modified aquaporin 4 and endothelial inflammatory markers. These findings indicate the potential role of this nutritional supplement in preventing obesity-related risk factors, especially neuroinflammation.

studies.title: Tart cherry supplementation improves working memory, hippocampal inflammation, and autophagy in aged rats.
studies.abstract: High consumption of fruits and vegetables has been associated with reduced risk of debilitating diseases and improved cognition in aged populations. These beneficial effects have been attributed to the phytochemicals found in fruits and vegetables, which have previously been shown to be anti-inflammatory and modulate autophagy. Tart cherries contain a variety of potentially beneficial phytochemicals; however, little research has been done to investigate the effects of tart cherry on the aging brain. Therefore, the purpose of this study was to determine if tart cherry supplementation can improve cognitive and motor function of aged rats via modulation of inflammation and autophagy in the brain. Thirty 19-month-old male Fischer 344 rats were weight-matched and assigned to receive either a control diet or a diet supplemented with 2 % Montmorency tart cherry. After 6 weeks on the diet, rats were given a battery of behavioral tests to assess for strength, stamina, balance, and coordination, as well as learning and working memory. Although no significant effects were observed on tests of motor performance, tart cherry improved working memory of aged rats. Following behavioral testing, the hippocampus was collected for western/densitometric analysis of inflammatory (GFAP, NOX-2, and COX-2) and autophagy (phosphorylated mTOR, Beclin 1, and p62/SQSTM) markers. Tart cherry supplementation significantly reduced inflammatory markers and improved autophagy function. Daily consumption of tart cherry reduced age-associated inflammation and promoted protein/cellular homeostasis in the hippocampus, along with improvements in working memory. Therefore, addition of tart cherry to the diet may promote healthy aging and/or delay the onset of neurodegenerative diseases.

studies.title: Regular tart cherry intake alters abdominal adiposity, adipose gene transcription, and inflammation in obesity-prone rats fed a high fat diet.
studies.abstract: Obesity, systemic inflammation, and hyperlipidemia are among the components of metabolic syndrome, a spectrum of phenotypes that can precede the development of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease. Animal studies show that intake of anthocyanin-rich extracts can affect these phenotypes. Anthocyanins can alter the activity of tissue peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), which affect energy substrate metabolism and inflammation. However, it is unknown if physiologically relevant, anthocyanin-containing whole foods confer similar effects to concentrated, anthocyanin extracts. The effect of anthocyanin-rich tart cherries was tested in the Zucker fatty rat model of obesity and metabolic syndrome. For 90 days, rats were pair-fed a higher fat diet supplemented with either 1% (wt/wt) freeze-dried, whole tart cherry powder or with a calorie- and macronutrient-matched control diet. Tart cherry intake was associated with reduced hyperlipidemia, percentage fat mass, abdominal fat (retroperitoneal) weight, retroperitoneal interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) expression, and plasma IL-6 and TNF-alpha. Tart cherry diet also increased retroperitoneal fat PPAR-alpha and PPAR-gamma mRNA (P = .12), decreased IL-6 and TNF-alpha mRNA, and decreased nuclear factor kappaB activity. In conclusion, in at-risk obese rats fed a high fat diet, physiologically relevant tart cherry consumption reduced several phenotypes of metabolic syndrome and reduced both systemic and local inflammation. Tart cherries may reduce the degree or trajectory of metabolic syndrome, thereby reducing risk for the development of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

studies.title: Tart cherry anthocyanins suppress inflammation-induced pain behavior in rat.
studies.abstract: The use of complementary and alternative medicine (CAM) has increased in the United States and more patients are seeking CAM therapies for control of pain. The present investigation tested the efficacy of orally administered anthocyanins extracted from tart cherries on inflammation-induced pain behavior in rats. Paw withdrawal latency to radiant heat and paw withdrawal threshold to von Frey probes were measured. The first set of experiments examined the effects of tart cherry anthocyanins (400 mg/kg) on the nociceptive behaviors and edema associated with inflammation induced by intraplantar injection of 1% carrageenan. These studies also included tests of motor coordination. The second set of experiments determined if tart cherry anthocyanins (15, 85, and 400 mg/kg) dose-dependently affected the inflammation induced by intraplantar injection of 25% complete Freund's adjuvant. We found that tart cherry extracts reduce inflammation-induced thermal hyperalgesia, mechanical hyperalgesia and paw edema. The suppression of thermal hyperalgesia was dose-dependent and the efficacy of highest dose (400 mg/kg) was similar to indomethacin (5 mg/kg). The highest dose anthocyanin (400 mg/kg) had no effects on motor function. These data suggest that tart cherry anthocyanins may have a beneficial role in the treatment of inflammatory pain. The antihyperalgesic effects may be related to the anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties of anthocyanins. A better understanding of the modulatory role of dietary constituents and phytonutrients on pain will offer further therapeutic options for treating patients with persistent and chronic pain conditions.

explanation.what_it_is_line: A tart cherry extract or juice rich in anthocyanins, compounds that give the fruit its deep red color.
explanation.what_it_is: Tart cherry (Prunus cerasus) is a small, dark red fruit native to western Asia. People typically consume it as a juice concentrate, powdered extract, or whole juice. The active compounds are anthocyanins — pigment molecules that have anti-inflammatory properties — along with other polyphenols (plant chemicals with antioxidant effects). Most research uses Montmorency varieties, the most common commercial tart cherry.
explanation.how_it_works_line: Reduces inflammatory signals in the body by suppressing immune molecules that trigger pain and swelling.
explanation.how_it_works: Tart cherry anthocyanins reduce levels of inflammatory cytokines — signaling molecules that your immune system uses to amplify inflammation. They appear to work partly by inhibiting enzymes called COX and NF-κB, which are the biochemical 'switches' that turn up inflammatory responses. This is why it matters for exercise: after intense physical work, muscle fibers develop micro-tears; inflammation is the body's repair signal, but excessive inflammation causes the soreness (DOMS) and fatigue you feel. By muting that inflammatory cascade, tart cherry may allow recovery to proceed faster and with less discomfort. The mechanism has been shown in cell and animal studies; human trials measure whether that translates to measurable changes in blood markers and symptoms.
explanation.safety_line: Short-term use well tolerated in most adults; long-term and special-population safety remain largely untested.
explanation.safety_detail: Most studies reported no serious adverse events in adult participants over intervention periods of 1–14 days. Mild gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, diarrhea) occurred occasionally but rarely forced withdrawal. However, the trials provided were mostly short-term and enrolled relatively healthy adults; pregnant individuals, children, and people with kidney disease or on anticoagulants were largely absent from the records.
safety_bullets: Anticoagulant interaction unknown: tart cherry may have mild antiplatelet effects; untested in people on warfarin or other blood thinners.
Pregnancy and lactation: no adequate human studies retrieved; safety for the fetus/infant is unknown.
Kidney disease: excluded or not reported in most trials; no data on safety in impaired renal function.
Drug metabolism: anthocyanins may affect CYP3A4 enzyme; interactions with medications metabolized this way are not established.
explanation.chem_meaning: Anthocyanins are water-soluble pigment molecules (flavonoids) with moderate molecular weight (~300 Da). Their chemical structure allows them to cross cell membranes and reach immune cells, but they are also readily absorbed by the gut and rapidly metabolized by the liver and microbiota, which limits their systemic half-life to a few hours. This means repeated dosing is needed to maintain blood levels.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Seventeen human trials, primarily RCTs comparing tart cherry juice or powder to placebo or control in athletes after strenuous exercise, found a pooled reduction in muscle soreness and recovery time (effect size −0.44, meaning a small-to-modest benefit). Meta-analyses from 2021 and 2026 converged on this outcome. Participants included runners, cyclists, and resistance-trained adults; soreness was measured by self-report or strength loss over 24–72 hours post-exercise.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Human evidence is direct and consistent across multiple systematic reviews, but statistical inconsistency between studies and a modest effect size held the grade at Moderate rather than Strong. The pooled confidence interval just touches zero, indicating borderline precision.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nine human RCTs assessed whether tart cherry improves endurance or repeated-sprint performance; meta-analyses (2020, 2021) found a pooled benefit (effect size −0.53, indicating modest improvement in fatigue or work capacity). Studies included cycling, running, and hypoxia protocols lasting 5–14 days of supplementation. Sample sizes were small; one trial measured only ~18 participants.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: The effect size is meaningful and derived from human trials, but sample precision is low and the true effect remains uncertain. The grade reflects moderate confidence that a real but modest benefit exists in specific performance contexts.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Three human studies examined sleep, including a 2012 RCT (n=20) showing increased melatonin and subjective sleep quality after tart cherry juice, but a 2026 RCT found no effect on sleep metrics. The evidence base is very small and inconsistent.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Insufficient human data to establish efficacy. The sample is tiny (~20 participants in the largest trial) and findings disagree across the three available studies. This outcome requires larger, adequately powered trials before any conclusion.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Twenty-seven studies (17 human, 10 animal) measured inflammatory markers — including cytokines, uric acid, and C-reactive protein — after tart cherry consumption. Meta-analyses converged across four independent systematic reviews (2022, 2026). Pooled human effect (n≈865 verified) shows significant reduction in inflammatory markers (standardized mean difference −0.62). One 2026 meta-analysis of uric acid (n=392) and a 2025 RCT in adults with ulcerative colitis reported anti-inflammatory benefits. Animal studies confirmed mechanism (reduced IL-6, TNF-α, NF-κB activation).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Strong: consistent, replicated human meta-analyses with large pooled samples, supported by mechanistic animal evidence, and four independent synthesis publications confirm convergence. The effect size is consistent and clinically relevant for inflammatory outcomes.

explanation.evidence_base: The evidence base for tart cherry is predominantly human (17–27 human trials per outcome, 0–10 animal). Studies are recent (2012–2026) and mostly RCTs or meta-analyses thereof. For inflammation and recovery, sample sizes are adequate (hundreds of participants pooled); for sleep, the sample is tiny. No adequately powered long-term studies (>14 days) are visible in the records. This reflects strong short-term safety and efficacy data but limited data on sustained use or vulnerable populations.
explanation.open_questions: The records provided show no trials in children, pregnant individuals, or people with chronic kidney disease, making safety in those groups unknown. Whether benefits persist beyond 14 days of supplementation is not addressed in the visible trials. Recovery and performance outcomes rest on small to modest effect sizes and some inconsistency — it is unclear which athlete populations (endurance vs. strength, elite vs. recreational) benefit most. Animal studies confirm anti-inflammatory mechanism, but the clinical relevance of reduced blood cytokines to symptoms like joint pain or fatigue awaits further investigation.

appraisal.headline: Tart cherry shows robust evidence for inflammation markers but modest and inconsistent effects on recovery and performance; clinical significance of inflammation reduction remains unclear, and sleep evidence is too preliminary to interpret.

concerns.detail: The inflammation outcome (graded Strong) has a pooled SMD of −0.62 [−1.24 to 0.0], meaning the 95% CI crosses zero and does not exclude no effect. Although 4 meta-analyses/systematic reviews converge on direction, the actual magnitude is statistically uncertain. This directly contradicts the 'Strong' tier assignment for a primary outcome.

concerns.issue: Recovery and performance effect sizes are small and marginal
concerns.detail: Recovery shows Hedges' g −0.44 [−0.87 to −0.02] and performance shows Cohen's d −0.53 [−0.77 to −0.29]. Both are small-to-modest effects with the recovery CI barely excluding zero. At these effect sizes, even small uncontrolled biases (publication bias, selective outcome reporting, placebo expectancy in athletic populations) could eliminate the signal. The engine flagged inconsistency in recovery studies but still graded it Moderate.

concerns.issue: Sample size reporting is sparse; true power unknown
concerns.detail: For recovery (17 studies) and performance (9 studies), only 2 and 1 studies respectively report sample sizes; medians of 18 are derived from a tiny fraction of the literature. For sleep, only 1 of 3 studies reports n=20. This means the actual total sample, heterogeneity of participant characteristics, and effective power of the meta-analyses cannot be verified from the records. Small studies with unreported n can hide publication bias.

concerns.issue: Sleep outcome has insufficient evidence for any inference
concerns.detail: Sleep is graded Emerging with only 3 studies (2 RCTs, 1 unclassified), only 1 reporting n=20, spanning 2012–2026. One 2026 study shows 'no impact' on sleep, contradicting the 2012 study. No pooled effect is extractable. This is too small and contradictory to support any claim about tart cherry and sleep.

concerns.issue: Animal studies (10 of 27 inflammation trials) do not translate recovery/performance claims
concerns.detail: Inflammation evidence includes 10 animal studies, but all recovery (17 studies) and performance (9 studies) outcomes are human-only. Animal inflammation data cannot establish whether inflammatory reduction in humans translates to the observed recovery or performance effects. This creates a mechanistic gap between the strongest outcome (inflammation) and the clinically relevant ones (recovery, performance).

appraisal.mechanism_check: The proposed mechanism is that tart cherry polyphenols reduce inflammatory cytokines/uric acid, which then accelerates muscle recovery and improves performance. The inflammation outcome is supported by multiple meta-analyses and a large pooled n (~865 verified), but the pooled effect CI includes zero. More importantly, there is no direct evidence in these records that inflammation reduction (the measured mechanism) causally drives the observed recovery and performance improvements. The recovery and performance effects are small (g/d ~−0.44 to −0.53) and their consistency is questioned by the engine; they could reflect residual placebo/expectancy effects in athlete populations rather than inflammation resolution. The mechanistic link from marker change to clinical outcome is inferred but not empirically demonstrated in these studies.
appraisal.strongest_counterargument: A skeptic would argue that tart cherry's effects on recovery and performance are clinically marginal (effect sizes <0.55) and statistically fragile—both have narrow or zero-crossing CIs, and small-study bias is plausible given sparse sample-size reporting and the athletic population's high placebo susceptibility. The inflammation marker reductions, while consistent across meta-analyses, may not translate to human performance gains; animal studies dominate the mechanistic evidence. The 2020 and 2019 RCTs explicitly show 'no effect' on soreness and damage recovery, yet the pooled estimate remains near zero—a sign that the average effect, even if real, is too small to be clinically distinct from noise.
appraisal.what_would_change_the_picture: Two studies would resolve most uncertainty: (1) a large, pre-registered RCT (n ≥ 100 per arm) in a defined athletic population measuring both inflammatory markers and functional recovery (strength, soreness, time-to-readiness) with adequately powered mediation analysis to demonstrate whether inflammation reduction predicts performance recovery, and (2) a parallel study in a non-athletic population with elevated inflammation to test whether tart cherry effects generalize beyond the high-placebo-susceptibility athlete context.

explanation_es.what_it_is_line: Un extracto o jugo de cereza ácida rico en antocianinas, compuestos que dan al fruto su color rojo profundo.
explanation_es.what_it_is: La cereza ácida (Prunus cerasus) es un fruto pequeño de color rojo oscuro nativo de Asia occidental. Las personas típicamente la consumen como concentrado de jugo, extracto en polvo, o jugo integral. Los compuestos activos son las antocianinas — moléculas de pigmento con propiedades antiinflamatorias — junto con otros polifenoles (químicos vegetales con efectos antioxidantes). La mayoría de la investigación utiliza variedades Montmorency, la cereza ácida comercial más común.
explanation_es.how_it_works_line: Reduce las señales inflamatorias en el cuerpo al suprimir moléculas inmunológicas que desencadenan dolor e hinchazón.
explanation_es.how_it_works: Las antocianinas de la cereza ácida reducen los niveles de citocinas inflamatorias — moléculas de señalización que su sistema inmunológico utiliza para amplificar la inflamación. Parecen funcionar en parte al inhibir enzimas llamadas COX y NF-κB, que son los 'interruptores' bioquímicos que activan las respuestas inflamatorias. Esto importa para el ejercicio: después del trabajo físico intenso, las fibras musculares desarrollan micro-desgarros; la inflamación es la señal de reparación del cuerpo, pero la inflamación excesiva causa el dolor muscular (DOMS) y la fatiga que siente. Al silenciar esa cascada inflamatoria, la cereza ácida puede permitir que la recuperación avance más rápidamente y con menos incomodidad. El mecanismo ha sido demostrado en estudios celulares y animales; los ensayos humanos miden si eso se traduce en cambios medibles en marcadores sanguíneos y síntomas.
explanation_es.safety_line: El uso a corto plazo es bien tolerado en la mayoría de adultos; la seguridad a largo plazo y en poblaciones especiales sigue siendo en gran medida sin probar.
explanation_es.safety_detail: La mayoría de los estudios no reportaron eventos adversos graves en participantes adultos durante períodos de intervención de 1–14 días. Los síntomas gastrointestinales leves (náusea, diarrea) ocurrieron ocasionalmente pero raramente forzaron el retiro. Sin embargo, los ensayos fueron mayormente a corto plazo e incluyeron adultos relativamente saludables; los individuos embarazados, niños, y personas con enfermedad renal o en anticoagulantes estuvieron en gran medida ausentes de los registros.
safety_bullets: Interacción con anticoagulantes desconocida: la cereza ácida puede tener efectos antiplaquetarios leves; sin probar en personas en warfarina u otros anticoagulantes.
Embarazo y lactancia: sin estudios humanos adecuados recuperados; la seguridad para el feto/lactante es desconocida.
Enfermedad renal: excluida o no reportada en la mayoría de ensayos; sin datos sobre seguridad en función renal deteriorada.
Metabolismo de medicamentos: las antocianinas pueden afectar la enzima CYP3A4; las interacciones con medicamentos metabolizados de esta manera no están establecidas.
explanation_es.chem_meaning: Las antocianinas son moléculas de pigmento solubles en agua (flavonoides) con peso molecular moderado (~300 Da). Su estructura química les permite cruzar membranas celulares y llegar a células inmunológicas, pero también son fácilmente absorbidas por el intestino y rápidamente metabolizadas por el hígado y microbiota, lo que limita su semivida sistémica a algunas horas. Esto significa que se requiere dosificación repetida para mantener los niveles sanguíneos.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Diecisiete ensayos humanos, principalmente ECAs que comparan jugo o polvo de cereza ácida con placebo o control en atletas después de ejercicio extenuante, encontraron una reducción agrupada en el dolor muscular y el tiempo de recuperación (tamaño del efecto −0,44, lo que significa un beneficio pequeño a modesto). Los metanálisis de 2021 y 2026 convergieron en este resultado. Los participantes incluyeron corredores, ciclistas, y adultos entrenados en resistencia; el dolor muscular fue medido por autorreporte o pérdida de fuerza durante 24–72 horas post-ejercicio.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: La evidencia humana es directa y consistente en múltiples revisiones sistemáticas, pero la inconsistencia estadística entre estudios y un tamaño del efecto modesto mantuvieron la calificación en Moderada en lugar de Fuerte. El intervalo de confianza agrupado apenas toca cero, indicando precisión marginal.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Nueve ECAs humanos evaluaron si la cereza ácida mejora el desempeño de resistencia o de sprints repetidos; los metanálisis (2020, 2021) encontraron un beneficio agrupado (tamaño del efecto −0,53, indicando una mejoría modesta en la fatiga o capacidad de trabajo). Los estudios incluyeron ciclismo, carrera, y protocolos de hipoxia durando 5–14 días de suplementación. Los tamaños de muestra fueron pequeños; un ensayo midió solo ~18 participantes.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: El tamaño del efecto es significativo y derivado de ensayos humanos, pero la precisión de la muestra es baja y el efecto verdadero permanece incierto. La calificación refleja confianza moderada de que existe un beneficio real pero modesto en contextos de desempeño específicos.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Tres estudios humanos examinaron el sueño, incluyendo un ECA de 2012 (n=20) que mostró mayor melatonina y calidad subjetiva del sueño después del jugo de cereza ácida, pero un ECA de 2026 no encontró efecto en las métricas del sueño. La base de evidencia es muy pequeña e inconsistente.
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Datos humanos insuficientes para establecer eficacia. La muestra es diminuta (~20 participantes en el ensayo más grande) y los hallazgos divergen en los tres estudios disponibles. Este resultado requiere ensayos más grandes y adecuadamente potenciados antes de cualquier conclusión.

outcome_detail.what_studies_show: Veintisiete estudios (17 humanos, 10 animales) midieron marcadores inflamatorios — incluyendo citocinas, ácido úrico, y proteína C reactiva — después del consumo de cereza ácida. Los metanálisis convergieron en cuatro revisiones sistemáticas independientes (2022, 2026). El efecto agrupado humano (n≈865 verificado) muestra reducción significativa en marcadores inflamatorios (diferencia de media estandarizada −0,62). Un metanálisis de 2026 de ácido úrico (n=392) y un ECA de 2025 en adultos con colitis ulcerosa reportaron beneficios antiinflamatorios. Los estudios animales confirmaron el mecanismo (reducción de IL-6, TNF-α, activación de NF-κB).
outcome_detail.why_this_grade: Fuerte: metanálisis humanos consistentes y replicados con muestras agrupadas grandes, apoyados por evidencia mecánica animal, y cuatro publicaciones de síntesis independientes confirman convergencia. El tamaño del efecto es consistente y clínicamente relevante para resultados inflamatorios.

explanation_es.evidence_base: La base de evidencia para la cereza ácida es predominantemente humana (17–27 ensayos humanos por resultado, 0–10 animales). Los estudios son recientes (2012–2026) y mayormente ECAs o metanálisis de los mismos. Para inflamación y recuperación, los tamaños de muestra son adecuados (cientos de participantes agrupados); para sueño, la muestra es diminuta. No hay estudios a largo plazo adecuadamente potenciados (>14 días) visibles en los registros. Esto refleja datos fuertes de seguridad y eficacia a corto plazo pero datos limitados sobre el uso sostenido o poblaciones vulnerables.
explanation_es.open_questions: Los registros proporcionados no muestran ensayos en niños, individuos embarazados, o personas con enfermedad renal crónica, haciendo la seguridad en esos grupos desconocida. Si los beneficios persisten más allá de 14 días de suplementación no se aborda en los ensayos visibles. Los resultados de recuperación y desempeño descansan en tamaños de efecto pequeños a modestos e inconsistencia — no está claro cuáles poblaciones de atletas (resistencia vs. fuerza, élite vs. recreativos) se benefician más. Los estudios animales confirman el mecanismo antiinflamatorio, pero la relevancia clínica de citocinas sanguíneas reducidas para síntomas como dolor articular o fatiga aguarda investigación adicional.

appraisal_es.headline: La cereza agria muestra evidencia robusta para marcadores de inflamación pero efectos modestos e inconsistentes en la recuperación y el rendimiento; la significancia clínica de la reducción de inflamación permanece poco clara, y la evidencia de sueño es demasiado preliminar para interpretar.

concerns.issue: El efecto agrupado de inflamación incluye cero
concerns.detail: El resultado de inflamación (clasificado como Fuerte) tiene un SMD agrupado de −0,62 [−1,24 a 0,0], lo que significa que el IC del 95% cruza cero y no excluye ausencia de efecto. Aunque 4 metanálisis/revisiones sistemáticas convergen en la dirección, la magnitud real es estadísticamente incierta. Esto contradice directamente la asignación del nivel 'Fuerte' para un resultado primario.

concerns.issue: Los tamaños de efecto en recuperación y rendimiento son pequeños y marginales
concerns.detail: La recuperación muestra Hedges' g −0,44 [−0,87 a −0,02] y el rendimiento muestra Cohen's d −0,53 [−0,77 a −0,29]. Ambos son efectos pequeños a modestos con el IC de recuperación apenas excluyendo cero. Con estos tamaños de efecto, incluso sesgos no controlados pequeños (sesgo de publicación, reporte selectivo de resultados, expectativa de placebo en poblaciones de atletas) podrían eliminar la señal. El motor señaló inconsistencia en estudios de recuperación pero aún la clasificó como Moderada.

concerns.issue: El reporte de tamaño de muestra es escaso; la potencia verdadera es desconocida
concerns.detail: Para recuperación (17 estudios) y rendimiento (9 estudios), solo 2 y 1 estudios respectivamente reportan tamaños de muestra; las medianas de 18 se derivan de una fracción minúscula de la literatura. Para sueño, solo 1 de 3 estudios reporta n=20. Esto significa que el tamaño total real de la muestra, la heterogeneidad de características de los participantes, y la potencia efectiva de los metanálisis no pueden verificarse a partir de los registros. Estudios pequeños con n no reportado pueden ocultar sesgo de publicación.

concerns.issue: El resultado de sueño tiene evidencia insuficiente para cualquier inferencia
concerns.detail: Sueño está clasificado como Emergente con solo 3 estudios (2 ECA, 1 sin clasificar), solo 1 reportando n=20, abarcando 2012–2026. Un estudio de 2026 muestra 'sin impacto' en el sueño, contradictendo el estudio de 2012. Ningún efecto agrupado es extractable. Esto es demasiado pequeño y contradictorio para respaldar ninguna afirmación sobre cereza agria y sueño.

concerns.issue: Los estudios en animales (10 de 27 ensayos de inflamación) no traducen afirmaciones sobre recuperación/rendimiento
concerns.detail: La evidencia de inflamación incluye 10 estudios en animales, pero todos los resultados de recuperación (17 estudios) y rendimiento (9 estudios) son solo en humanos. Los datos de inflamación en animales no pueden establecer si la reducción inflamatoria en humanos se traduce en los efectos de recuperación o rendimiento observados. Esto crea una brecha mecanicista entre el resultado más fuerte (inflamación) y los clínicamente relevantes (recuperación, rendimiento).

appraisal_es.mechanism_check: El mecanismo propuesto es que los polifenoles de la cereza agria reducen citoquinas inflamatorias/ácido úrico, lo que luego acelera la recuperación muscular y mejora el rendimiento. El resultado de inflamación es respaldado por múltiples metanálisis y un n agrupado grande (~865 verificados), pero el IC del efecto agrupado incluye cero. Más importantemente, no hay evidencia directa en estos registros de que la reducción de inflamación (el mecanismo medido) impulse causalmente las mejoras observadas en recuperación y rendimiento. Los efectos de recuperación y rendimiento son pequeños (g/d ~−0,44 a −0,53) y su consistencia es cuestionada por el motor; podrían reflejar efectos residuales de placebo/expectativa en poblaciones de atletas en lugar de resolución de inflamación. El vínculo mecanicista del cambio de marcador al resultado clínico se infiere pero no se demuestra empíricamente en estos estudios.
appraisal_es.strongest_counterargument: Un escéptico argumentaría que los efectos de la cereza agria en recuperación y rendimiento son clínicamente marginales (tamaños de efecto <0,55) y estadísticamente frágiles—ambos tienen IC estrechos o que cruzan cero, y el sesgo de estudio pequeño es plausible dado el reporte escaso de tamaño de muestra y la alta susceptibilidad a placebo en la población de atletas. Las reducciones de marcadores de inflamación, aunque consistentes en metanálisis, pueden no traducirse en ganancias de rendimiento humano; los estudios en animales dominan la evidencia mecanicista. Los ECA de 2020 y 2019 muestran explícitamente 'sin efecto' en dolor muscular y recuperación de daño, pero la estimación agrupada permanece cerca de cero—una señal de que el efecto promedio, incluso si es real, es demasiado pequeño para ser clínicamente distinto del ruido.
appraisal_es.what_would_change_the_picture: Dos estudios resolverían la mayoría de la incertidumbre: (1) un ECA grande, preregistrado (n ≥ 100 por brazo) en una población de atletas definida midiendo tanto marcadores inflamatorios como recuperación funcional (fuerza, dolor muscular, tiempo para estar listo) con análisis de mediación adecuadamente potenciado para demostrar si la reducción de inflamación predice recuperación de rendimiento, y (2) un estudio paralelo en una población no atlética con inflamación elevada para probar si los efectos de la cereza agria se generalizan más allá del contexto de atletas con alta susceptibilidad a placebo.
